title: Voice as Body Language
hook: Your voice is the part of your body people can hear in the dark, carrying your breath, tension and pace ahead of your words.
why:
Most books about body language barely mention the voice, as if it belonged to language and not to the body. It belongs to both. A voice is made by breath pushed from the lungs, shaped by muscles in the throat, and filtered through the mouth and nose. When the body tightens, so does the voice. When breathing changes, the voice changes with it. And unlike the face, the voice cannot be checked in a mirror, so most people have far less control over it than they think.

This chapter teaches you to hear the body in the voice. You will learn how quickly people form impressions from a voice, how well feelings can be heard and how often they are misheard, what stress does to pitch and pace, why pitch carries rank, what pauses and fillers actually signal, how moods travel by voice from one person to another, and why listening with your eyes closed can sharpen what you hear. As always, the aim is to describe what you hear before deciding what it means, and to read every voice against its own baseline.

teach.h: The voice is a body part, and people judge it fast.
teach.p:
In 1958 the linguist George Trager gave a name to everything in speech that is not the words themselves: paralanguage. It includes pitch, volume, pace, rhythm, the quality of the voice, breathiness, tension, pauses, and the small sounds people make between words, such as sighs, laughs and fillers. Everything a voice does besides carrying the words is body language you can hear.

People judge it remarkably quickly. In 2014 Phil McAleer, Alexander Todorov and Pascal Belin played listeners recordings of strangers saying a single word, *hello*, and asked them to rate the speakers on traits such as trustworthiness and dominance. Listeners agreed with each other to a striking degree, from less than a second of speech. Whether those impressions were accurate is a different question, and one the study did not set out to answer. But they form, and they shape how the speaker is treated.

This means two things for a reader. When you hear someone, you are forming an impression of them from their voice before you have weighed a word they said, and that impression may be no more than a stereotype about accent, pitch or pace. It deserves the same suspicion as a first impression of a face.

And when you speak, you are being judged the same way. Your voice carries your breath, your tension and your pace to listeners who may never see you, on the phone, in the next room, in the dark. The chapter on video review of yourself in Part VI is the best way to hear what they hear.

Listen to the voice as a body, before you listen to it as a message.
teach.disconfirm: If listeners' impressions from a single word turned out to differ wildly from one listener to the next, voice impressions would be weaker than this block suggests. The *hello* study found strong agreement, which is what makes the stereotype risk worth taking seriously.

teach.p:
In 1996 Rainer Banse and Klaus Scherer recorded actors expressing fourteen different emotions through the same meaningless sentences, so that only the voice could carry the feeling. Listeners identified the intended emotion far more often than chance, and acoustic analysis showed why: anger tended to be loud and high with sharp onsets, sadness quiet, low and slow, fear high and fast, contentment soft and relaxed.

In 2003 Patrik Juslin and Petri Laukka reviewed over a hundred studies of emotion in voices. Recognition was well above chance on average, comparable in some studies to recognition from faces. It was somewhat lower when speaker and listener came from different cultures, and some emotions were much easier to hear than others. Anger and sadness were usually easy. Disgust and fear were often confused with other emotions.

Two cautions apply. First, most of these studies used actors, who produce clearer and stronger vocal expressions than people usually do in ordinary life. Real voices carry feelings more faintly and more mixed. Second, the same acoustic pattern can arise from different states. A loud, fast, high voice may be anger, excitement, fear or simply a noisy room. A quiet, slow, low voice may be sadness, fatigue, calm, concentration or a cold.

So voices give you real information about feeling, at roughly the same level of reliability as faces, and with the same need for baseline and context. What changed in this voice, compared with how this person usually sounds, and when?

Hear the change first. The feeling comes later, and with a question mark.
teach.disconfirm: If listeners could identify feelings from voices in ordinary conversation as accurately as from acted recordings, voices would be better guides than this block allows. The gap between acted and everyday speech is a reason for caution.

teach.h: Stress tightens and lifts the voice.
teach.p:
Under stress, breathing tends to become faster and higher in the chest, and the muscles of the neck, jaw and throat tighten. The voice follows. Reviews of the research on vocal signs of stress find that pitch tends to rise, the voice often becomes tighter or more breathy, and speech may speed up or become more halting. These changes are not universal; some people become slower, quieter and flatter under strain, and the pattern varies with the kind of stress.

That variation is why the baseline matters so much for voices. A man whose voice rises and quickens whenever he talks about something he cares about is not necessarily stressed when it does so. A man whose voice is usually animated and goes flat and slow has changed, and the change may matter more than any particular feature.

Stammering deserves special care. Around one in a hundred adults stammers, and for many the stammer becomes more frequent under pressure: in meetings, on the phone, when saying their own name. A stammer under pressure is not a sign of evasion or uncertainty about what the person is saying. It is a sign that the situation is harder for them than it looks, and the kind response is to wait, without finishing their words for them.

Your own voice under stress is one of the earliest signs your body gives you, and one of the easiest to work with. The chapter on reading yourself under stress in Part VI describes the long breath out before speaking. It lowers and steadies the voice, and the people listening hear the difference.
teach.disconfirm: If people's voices did not change in any consistent way between calm and stressful conversations, against their own baselines, the stress signs in this block would be unreliable. Compare a recording of yourself in each kind of conversation before deciding.
teach.pullQuote: A tight voice is often the first place stress becomes audible.

teach.p:
Lower voices tend to be heard as more dominant, and this link appears in both how voices are judged and how people use them. In 2006 David Puts, Steven Gaulin and Katherine Verdolini recorded men taking part in what they believed was a competition for a lunch date. Men who rated themselves as physically more dominant than their competitor tended to lower their voice pitch when speaking to him, and men who rated themselves as less dominant tended to raise it.

Listeners respond to the same cue. In 2012 Casey Klofstad, Rindy Anderson and Susan Peters asked people to choose between pairs of recorded voices saying the same sentence, one slightly lower than the other, as candidates for leadership. They tended to choose the lower voice, both for men and for women.

This is a bias worth naming. It means that people with naturally higher voices, including many women and some men, may be heard as less authoritative regardless of what they say. A reader who knows this can correct for it: notice when a voice's pitch, rather than its content, is shaping your sense of who is in charge.

Pitch also moves within a conversation, and the movement is more informative than the level. A man whose voice drops when he reaches the decision he has made is closing the matter. A voice that rises at the end of a statement may be inviting a response, signalling uncertainty, or simply following a regional or generational habit. A voice that climbs steadily through an argument may be losing its footing.

Hear the pitch, then check whether it is telling you about rank or only about the larynx.
teach.disconfirm: If, in groups where you know the hierarchy, the people with the lowest voices were no more likely than others to be treated as leaders, the pitch bias would not be operating in your setting. Watch for it in a few meetings before assuming either way.

teach.h: Pauses and fillers are the sound of thinking.
teach.p:
Every speaker pauses, and the pauses are informative. In the 1960s Frieda Goldman-Eisler found that pauses in spontaneous speech cluster before the points where speakers have to make choices: a new idea, an unusual word, a difficult sentence. Pauses are the sound of planning, and harder thinking produces more of them.

Fillers do similar work. In 2002 Herbert Clark and Jean Fox Tree analysed large collections of recorded conversation and found that *uh* and *um* are not random noise. Speakers tend to use *uh* to signal a short delay and *um* to signal a longer one, and both help hold the floor: they tell listeners that the speaker has not finished and is still working on what comes next.

This undoes a common misreading. A person who pauses, says *um* and restarts a sentence while answering a question is usually showing you that the question is hard, or that they are choosing their words with care. It does not show that they are uncertain of the facts, still less that they are making things up. The chapter on deception explains why no voice feature reliably signals lying.

Silence after a question is similar. Many people rush to fill it, rephrasing the question or answering it themselves. A few seconds of silence is often the time the other person needs to think, and the answer that follows is usually better. Part III takes up silence as communication in its own right.

When someone pauses, the kind thing and the informative thing are the same: wait.
teach.disconfirm: If people's pauses and fillers turned out to be no more frequent on harder questions than on easy ones, against their own baseline, the planning explanation would be weak. Ask a friend a few of each and listen.

teach.h: Voices carry moods from one person to another.
teach.p:
In 2000 Roland Neumann and Fritz Strack asked people to listen to a philosophical text read aloud in a slightly happy or slightly sad voice. The content was identical. Listeners who heard the happy reading came away in a better mood than those who heard the sad one, and when asked to read the text aloud themselves, they tended to echo the tone they had heard. Neither group was aware of the effect.

This is the vocal side of the emotional contagion described in the final chapter of Part VI. People tend to match the pace, pitch and loudness of those they talk with, and feelings travel with the match. It is why a calm voice can help steady an anxious person and a tense one can unsettle a whole room.

For a reader, contagion cuts both ways. When a conversation gets louder and faster, it is worth asking whether both people are now tense, or whether one of them simply caught the other's pace. And when you find yourself suddenly anxious after a phone call, part of what you are feeling may be the caller's voice in your own body.

For a speaker, it offers a lever. You cannot argue someone into calm, but you can lower your own voice, slow your pace and let your breath settle, and the other person will often follow. The chapter on high-stakes environments in Part VI describes this in tense encounters. It works in ordinary ones too: a parent's voice at bedtime, a manager's on a bad day.

Your voice is part of the weather in every room you speak in.
teach.disconfirm: If people's moods did not shift at all when you deliberately spoke more calmly or more tensely, by their own account and by how they sounded, vocal contagion would be weak in your relationships. Try it in low-stakes conversations and ask afterwards.

teach.p:
When you can see a face, it dominates your attention, and you hear voices less well. In 2017 Michael Kraus reported a set of studies in which people judged others' feelings more accurately when they could only hear them than when they could both see and hear them. The finding needs repeating by other researchers before it can carry much weight, but it fits a common experience: phone calls and conversations in the dark can feel unusually intimate, and people sometimes notice things in a voice that a face would have covered.

You can use this deliberately. On the phone, close your eyes or look at a blank wall instead of a screen. In a recording, listen once without the picture. In person, when something seems to be going on, let your gaze rest on the table for a moment and attend only to the voice.

Describe what you hear in terms of the voice itself. Is it higher or lower than usual for this person, faster or slower, louder or quieter? Is the rhythm smooth or halting? Is the breath audible? Are there more pauses, or fewer? Is the voice tight, breathy, flat, warm? Then, as always, note the moment the change began.

Voice is also the channel people are least able to monitor in themselves, which makes it a useful partner to the face. A smile that arrives with a flat, slow voice is a disagreement between channels worth noticing, though, as the chapter on clusters showed, it is often mixed feeling rather than concealment.

Sometimes the best way to read someone is to stop looking at them.
teach.disconfirm: If, over several weeks, your readings of people's feelings on voice-only calls turned out less accurate than your readings face to face, checked against what they later told you, voice-only listening would not suit you. Keep a short record before deciding.

poseGallery.doCaption: One breath out, then the answer.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Answering with a high, held breath.
poseGallery.annotation: Stress tightens and lifts the voice. A long breath out before speaking lowers and steadies it, and listeners hear the difference.

poseGallery.doCaption: Waiting through it, and hearing what he says.
poseGallery.annotation: Stammering often increases under pressure. It tells you the situation is hard for the speaker, not that he is hiding anything.

poseGallery.doCaption: Nothing else in front of you; just the voice.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Half-listening on a call while scrolling.
poseGallery.annotation: A face, or a screen, pulls attention from the voice. Some things are easier to hear with nothing to look at.

poseGallery.doCaption: Pausing, and letting the point land.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Racing through it, filling every silence.
poseGallery.annotation: Pauses are the sound of thinking, for speakers and listeners both. Silence after a question often brings the better answer.

caseStudy:
Steve, fifty-three, phones his son Liam every Sunday. Liam is nineteen and in his first year at university two hundred miles away. On the phone Liam is usually fast and loud, interrupting himself with stories, laughing at his own jokes.

One Sunday in November, Steve notices something before he notices anything Liam says. Liam's voice is lower than usual and flat. He answers in short sentences with long pauses before each one. There is no laughter. When Steve asks how things are going, Liam says *fine, yeah, fine*, and the words come slowly, with a breath before them.

Steve has been practising listening with his eyes closed on these calls, and he does it now. Every feature of the voice has changed from Liam's baseline at once, pitch, pace, rhythm, laughter, and the change began from the first word. It is not the line; he can hear the television in the background clearly.

He considers the rivals. Liam might be tired, or ill, or hungover, or in the middle of exams. Any of those could flatten a voice. He decides not to press on the phone, where Liam can hang up, and not to tell him that he sounds low, which might make him defensive. Instead he says he will be driving past the university on Saturday for work, which is almost true, and asks if Liam fancies lunch.

At lunch, side by side in a busy café, Liam tells him that his exams went badly, that he has not made many friends, and that most evenings he sits in his room. They talk for two hours. Steve helps him find the university's advice service and a climbing club that meets on Wednesdays.

On the following Sunday, Liam's voice is quicker. Not back to normal. Quicker.
observe: On your next phone call, close your eyes for part of it and notice the other person's pitch, pace, pauses and breath.
Notice your own voice the next time you are under pressure, and whether it rises, quickens, tightens or goes flat.
In a meeting, notice whose voices sound most authoritative to you, and ask yourself whether that comes from what they say or how low they speak.

drills.name: Voice Baselines
steps: Choose three people you speak with often, in person or on the phone.
For each, write a short description of their usual voice: pitch, pace, volume, rhythm and laughter.
Note anything that usually changes when they are excited, tired or annoyed.
Over the next week, listen for any change from these baselines.
Record each change, the moment it began, and two possible causes.

drills.name: Sound Only
steps: Choose a recorded interview of someone answering unscripted questions.
Listen to five minutes without the picture and note every change in pitch, pace, pauses and breath.
Write what you think the speaker was feeling at each change.
Watch the same five minutes with the picture and note how your impressions change.
Write down which impressions came from the voice alone.

drills.name: Pause Tolerance
steps: In your next few conversations, after asking a question, count silently to five before speaking again.
Notice the urge to fill the silence and resist it.
Note whether the answer that comes is longer or more thoughtful than usual.
Note any fillers the other person uses while thinking, without judging them.
Write one sentence about how the silences felt to you.

drills.name: Your Voice Under Pressure
steps: Record yourself reading a short paragraph aloud while calm.
Then record yourself describing a recent frustrating situation as if to the person involved.
Listen to both and note differences in pitch, pace, volume and breath.
Record the frustrating description again after one long breath out, speaking a little slower.
Compare the second and third recordings and note what changed.

drills.name: Calm Contagion
steps: Choose a low-stakes conversation where the other person is mildly stressed, such as a colleague with a deadline.
Deliberately lower your voice slightly and slow your pace, without commenting on it.
Notice whether their voice changes over the next few minutes.
Afterwards, note what happened to your own state as well.
Repeat in two more conversations and compare.

quiz.q: A colleague pauses and says um several times while answering your question. What does the research on pauses and fillers suggest?
options: That he is unsure of the facts, and his answer is probably wrong
That he is making the answer up as he goes, so check it carefully
That he is planning what to say; fillers signal a coming delay
That he is nervous of you personally, and wants the meeting to end
quiz.explain: Pauses cluster where speakers have to make choices, and fillers signal a delay while holding the floor. More of them usually means a harder question or more careful wording, not uncertainty or invention.

quiz.q: What did Puts, Gaulin and Verdolini find in men who believed they were physically more dominant than their competitor?
options: They tended to lower the pitch of their voices when speaking to him
They spoke a great deal more loudly than the other men in the study
They spoke noticeably faster, and interrupted their competitor more
They stopped speaking to their competitor and addressed others instead
quiz.explain: Men who saw themselves as more dominant lowered their pitch, and those who saw themselves as less dominant raised it. Pitch carries rank, in how people speak and in how they are heard.

quiz.q: What did Juslin and Laukka's review of over a hundred studies find about recognising emotions from voices?
options: Recognition was close to perfect for every emotion that was studied
Recognition was no better than chance, whatever the emotion or culture
Only trained actors could recognise emotions in other people's voices
Recognition was well above chance, and a little lower across cultures
quiz.explain: Voices carry real information about feeling, at roughly the reliability of faces, but most studies used actors, and some emotions are often confused. Baseline and context are as necessary here as anywhere.

quiz.q: A new colleague stammers much more in meetings than in one-to-one chats. A manager concludes that he is evasive in meetings. What fits?
options: Agree, since a stammer that changes with the setting shows he is hiding
Stammering often rises under pressure; it is not a sign of evasion
Suggest he prepare scripts so that he can avoid stammering in meetings
Finish his sentences for him in meetings so that nobody has to wait
quiz.explain: For many people who stammer, pressure makes it more frequent. It tells you the setting is harder for him, not that he is concealing anything. Waiting, without finishing his words, is the kind response.

quiz.q: What did Neumann and Strack find when people listened to a text read in a slightly happy or slightly sad voice?
options: Listeners' moods were unaffected, since the content was identical
Listeners only noticed the tone if they had been told to listen for it
Listeners' moods shifted towards the tone of the voice they had heard
Listeners disliked the reader and remembered less of the content
quiz.explain: Moods travelled with the voice, without listeners noticing. This vocal contagion is why a calm voice can steady a room and a tense one can unsettle it.

quiz.q: On the phone, your son, usually fast and loud, speaks slowly and flatly with long pauses, and says he is fine. What fits this chapter?
options: Note the change from his baseline, and find a gentle way to ask more
Take him at his word, since he has told you plainly that he is fine
Tell him straight away that he sounds depressed and needs some help
Assume the phone line is poor and talk to him again next week instead
quiz.explain: Every feature of his voice has changed from his own baseline at once. It does not tell you why, but it is worth a low-pressure way to ask more, such as meeting in person, rather than either ignoring it or labelling it.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person whose voice you know well, a partner, a parent, a friend, a colleague. Describe their usual voice in terms of pitch, pace, volume and laughter. Then recall one moment when their voice changed before their words told you anything. What changed, and what did it turn out to mean, if you found out? Finally, think about your own voice: what do you think it does under pressure, and how could you find out for certain?
reflection.guidance: Most people find it easier to describe a change in a familiar voice than to describe the voice itself, which is a sign of how much we hear without attending to it. The last question is the one to act on. A recording of yourself in a tense conversation, made with everyone's agreement, is the surest way to hear what others hear.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to ignore the voice altogether, watching faces while the most informative channel goes unheard. The second is to read voice features as if they were a dictionary: fillers as uncertainty, pauses as evasion, a stammer as guilt, a low voice as authority. The third is to let pitch bias decide who sounds credible, so that people with higher voices are heard as less serious whatever they say. The fourth is to forget your own voice, which is carrying your breath and tension to everyone you speak to, and spreading your mood whether you mean it to or not. Describe the voice, compare it with its baseline, note the moment it changed, and wait through the silences.
